articles.title: US midterms: Indian-origin Democrat Pia Dandiya wins Florida House race
articles.summary: Indian-origin Democrat Pia Dandiya has won Florida's 22nd Congressional District race, defeating Republican candidate Casey Askar in one of South
articles.body: Indian-origin Democrat Pia Dandiya has won Florida's 22nd Congressional District race, defeating Republican candidate Casey Askar in one of South Florida's closely watched contests in the 2026 US midterm elections, CBS News projected.Dandiya's victory marks a significant milestone for the Indian-American community. She becomes the first Indian-American to be elected to the US House of Representatives from Florida and the 10th Indian-American elected to the US Congress, according to reports.Born and raised in Palm Beach County to Indian immigrant parents, Dandiya is a former teacher and high school principal in Harlem. She has also served as a White House Fellow and worked at Apple. Her campaign focused on education, affordability and economic opportunity.She will represent Florida's newly redrawn 22nd Congressional District, which stretches across parts of Palm Beach, Broward, Hendry and Collier counties. The district was reshaped in May 2026 as part of Republican Governor Ron DeSantis' congressional redistricting effort ahead of the midterm elections.Dandiya is among the Indian-American candidates making electoral gains in the November 3 elections. Democrat Suhas Subramanyam has secured re-election from Virginia's 10th Congressional District, with NBC News projecting his victory. He defeated Republican challenger Dave Beckwith and independent candidate Ahsen Malik, winning a second term in the US House of Representatives.Read more: Indian-origin Suhas Subramanyam wins re-election to US House from VirginiaMeanwhile, Indian-American Democrat Aruna Miller has also secured re-election as Maryland's lieutenant governor. She ran alongside Governor Wes Moore, whose re-election was projected by NBC News.Other prominent Indian-origin candidates in the elections include Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who is contesting the Ohio governor's race, and Democratic incumbents Ro Khanna, Ami Bera and Pramila Jayapal, who are seeking re-election to the US House.The November 3 elections are being held halfway through President Donald Trump's four-year term and will determine the balance of power in the US Congress for the next two years.All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are being contested. Voters are also electing governors in 36 states.The results will determine whether Republicans retain control of both chambers or Democrats make gains and take control of Congress, potentially affecting Trump's legislative agenda during the remaining two years of his presidency.You use AI every day. articles.title: US election results: Amy Acton defeats Donald Trump-backed Vivek Ramaswamy to become Ohio's first woman governor
articles.summary: Democrat Dr Amy Acton has won the race for governor of Ohio, defeating Trump-backed Indian-American Republican candidate, Vivek Ramaswamy, to become the
articles.body: Democrat Dr Amy Acton has won the race for governor of Ohio, defeating Trump-backed Indian-American Republican candidate, Vivek Ramaswamy, to become the first woman elected to the state's top office.Her victory also marks the first time in 20 years that a Democrat has won the governorship.Acton, a public health physician and former Ohio health director during the Covid-19 pandemic, overcame more than $100 million spent against her by Ramaswamy and his Republican allies.She will succeed Republican Governor Mike DeWine, who is barred from seeking another term.The 60-year-old built her campaign around affordability and improved access to healthcare, appealing to working- and middle-class voters by highlighting her personal background. An Ohio native, Acton has spoken about spending part of her childhood homeless and living in a tent for one winter.Her victory comes as Democrats seek to regain ground in Ohio, where voters have increasingly shifted towards Republicans during Donald Trump's political rise.Acton capitalises on affordability concerns and Ramaswamy's wealthActon's campaign sought to portray Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and former 2024 presidential candidate, as out of touch with ordinary voters facing higher living costs.The campaign highlighted concerns over the cost of living, fuel prices and the impact of Trump's tariffs. Ramaswamy and his Republican allies spent more than $100 million during the contest.Billionaire Elon Musk also contributed at least $5 million to a political action committee aligned with the Republican candidate, according to the AP.Acton won despite repeated campaign appearances by Trump and Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native, who travelled to the state in the final weeks to rally support for Ramaswamy and Republican Senator Jon Husted.Ramaswamy had secured early backing from Ohio Republicans, with DeWine appointing Husted, then the leading Republican contender for governor, to the US Senate after Vance vacated the seat to become vice-president.The decision to endorse Ramaswamy, a newcomer to Ohio politics, forced several established Republican politicians, including the state attorney general and treasurer, to reconsider their political plans.Ramaswamy also faced resistance during the Republican primary from Casey “The Car Guy” Putsch, a vehicle designer and YouTube personality whose campaign attracted nearly 18 per cent of the Republican vote despite spending only $130,000. Putsch later announced that he planned to vote for Acton.Attack ad featuring Acton's estranged mother sparks backlashThe campaign was also marked by controversy over an advertisement aired by Ramaswamy in its final month. The 60-second spot featured Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her upbringing and urging voters not to support her.Arthur called Acton “a liar” with a “serious problem” with being honest about her past. The advertisement drew criticism after details emerged about the family's history. Arthur had been estranged from Acton for nearly 50 years and had lost custody of her children after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was a child.The man pleaded not guilty and fled the state before he could stand trial, the AP reported.The advertisement initially surfaced online before Ramaswamy claimed responsibility for it. He defended the campaign as a criticism of what he described as a pattern of deception by Acton, disputing claims that it questioned whether she had been abused as a child.Trump and Vance defended Ramaswamy's decision to use the advertisement. Trump also expressed jealousy that he had never had the opportunity to run a similar attack against a political rival.However, the advertisement triggered bipartisan criticism, including from five former Ohio governors, senior politicians from both parties, women's groups and several hundred alumni of Ramaswamy's Catholic high school in Cincinnati. Critics described it as gutter politics and called on him to withdraw it.The campaign eventually took the advertisement off the air about a week before Election Day, after spending roughly a quarter of the $4 million advertising budget it had announced.Former pandemic health director returns to state leadershipActon became one of Ohio Democrats' most recognisable figures during the early months of the Covid-19 pandemic, when she appeared in statewide broadcasts alongside DeWine and Husted.During the campaign, Ramaswamy and his allies criticised her role in the state's pandemic response, arguing that she had been too aggressive in shutting down schools and businesses. DeWine defended his former health director, saying responsibility for the decisions ultimately rested with him, although he continued to endorse Ramaswamy.Acton enters the governor's office without having previously held elected office. Her predecessor, DeWine, is 79 and is expected to retire from electoral politics after five decades in public life.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: North Korea fires missiles hours after rejecting US accusations over Binance hack
articles.summary: North Korea fired multiple missiles towards the sea off its eastern coast on Wednesday, South Korea's military said, hours after Pyongyang ruled out
articles.body: North Korea fired multiple missiles towards the sea off its eastern coast on Wednesday, South Korea's military said, hours after Pyongyang ruled out resuming talks with Washington over accusations that North Korean hackers were behind a major cryptocurrency theft from Binance.The launches came amid renewed tensions between the two countries, with North Korea accusing the US of pursuing a hostile policy and saying it had no reason to engage in dialogue with Washington.South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said it had detected several missiles being fired towards North Korea's eastern waters.South Korean and US authorities were analysing details of the launches, it said, adding that Seoul remained prepared to respond to any potential provocations under its alliance with Washington.North Korea rejects US accusations over Binance hackThe missile launches followed North Korea's denial of involvement in the hacking of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The exchange said on Friday that hackers had stolen more than $6 billion, in what appeared to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.The FBI subsequently attributed the attack to North Korean hackers, identifying the hacking group as TraderTraitor. The group was also held responsible for a $1.5 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Bybit last year.Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and a senior official, issued a statement on Wednesday rejecting the FBI's allegations and describing the announcement as “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” North Korea.Pyongyang dismissed the accusation as “a trite provocation”.“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” Kim Yo Jong said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”She also ruled out dialogue with Washington until the US abandoned what she described as its hostile policy towards North Korea.Weapons tests continue amid uncertainty over US talksNorth Korea has stepped up its weapons testing in recent months, following Trump's expressed interest in restoring diplomacy with Kim Jong Un. Observers cited by the news agency AP said Pyongyang was likely seeking to pressure Washington into dropping its hostile policy and offering concessions before any resumption of talks.Recent North Korean weapons tests have included a submarine-launched ballistic missile, hypersonic missiles, attack drones and cluster bombs designed to be carried by ballistic missiles.Pyongyang said on Tuesday that it had tested a new cluster warhead for strategic cruise missiles a day earlier. It claimed the weapon could destroy an area of five to six hectares (12 to 15 acres) with “high-density power”.North Korea had also conducted a series of missile tests this year, including one launch in which a missile travelled more than 900 km. Wednesday's launch appeared to be its fourth missile test in the past month.Lee Choon-geun, a missile expert and board member at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, said the frequent tests could indicate that North Korea was preparing for mass production and deployment of missiles, potentially including weapons for export to Russia.“Before mass production and deployment, you typically need many tests,” Lee said. “Or they may be looking to export missiles in bulk to Russia, in which case they would need to run a lot of tests before shipping.”Tensions rise along inter-Korean borderTensions between North and South Korea have also increased following mine explosions near their shared border in September that injured three South Korean soldiers.Seoul accused Pyongyang of planting the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. North Korea denied responsibility and warned of retaliation if provoked.Pyongyang later threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy additional weapons systems along the border.The latest missile launches also followed a report in North Korean state media that Kim Jong Un had visited a naval shipyard where a destroyer was being built and stressed the importance of developing a powerful naval force.You use AI every day. articles.title: Singer Sia secretly gave more than $1 million to 19 Survivor contestants over eight years, including players who never won the show
articles.summary: For eight years, Survivor contestants had something to look forward to beyond the competition's usual prize money.
articles.body: For eight years, Survivor contestants had something to look forward to beyond the competition's usual prize money. Singer Sia, a longtime admirer of the reality series, developed an unusual tradition of giving cash directly to players who caught her attention. The recipients were not necessarily the contestants who made it to the final or walked away with the show's grand prize. Some had become memorable for their behaviour, personal stories or individual moments during the competition. As reported, by the time the arrangement ended, the singer had distributed more than $1 million among 19 contestants across 14 seasons, creating a separate source of financial recognition within the long-running television franchise.Sia's unexpected $50,000 reward at the 2016 Survivor finaleAccording to Survivor host, Jeff Probst Instagram story in 2024, the story began at the live finale of Survivor: Kaoh Rong in 2016. Sia was in the audience when she noticed contestant Tai Trang, whose conduct during the competition had particularly impressed her. Trang had shown concern for a chicken that was at risk of being eaten by the other contestants, an episode that caught the singer's attention.Rather than simply expressing her appreciation, Sia decided to give him $50,000 from her own money. The gesture was unexpected, even for those involved in the programme. It was not part of the show's established prize structure, and there had been no indication that a celebrity audience member might offer a contestant a personal financial reward.How Sia chose contestants for her cash rewardsThe arrangement differed from the usual financial rewards associated with Survivor. Contestants compete for a substantial cash prize, with the eventual winner determined through the show's final voting process. Sia's contributions operated separately from that system.Her choices were based on her own reactions to individual players rather than their final positions in the competition. This meant that contestants did not have to win the series, reach the final stages or even become the season's central personality to receive money from her.Over the years, the amounts varied considerably. Individual gifts reportedly ranged from approximately $14,000 to $100,000, depending on the contestant and Sia's decision. Her selections also gave attention to players whose contributions to a season might otherwise have gone without a separate financial reward.Jeff Probst helped communicate Sia's choices to contestantsSurvivor host Jeff Probst was closely involved in the process of delivering the awards. In a December 2022 interview with Entertainment Weekly, he described how Sia would watch the season finale and communicate which contestant she wanted to reward.During the programme's earlier live reunion format, the singer sometimes watched from the audience or from Probst's dressing room. Once she had decided on a recipient, she would inform the host, who helped ensure the contestant received the money.The recipients could learn about the gift immediately, making the announcement a separate moment during the show's finale proceedings. Probst described the experience as an opportunity to watch Sia make her own decisions about who should receive the money.He also made clear that the contributions came from the singer herself. They were not an additional payment funded by the network or part of the show's official prize arrangements.Sia explained why she often gave contestants $15,000Although the amounts were not fixed, Sia had previously discussed her preference for giving approximately $15,000 in certain circumstances. She explained that this was generally the highest amount she could offer without the recipient having to pay taxes on the gift, according to her understanding of the applicable rules. Her awards were not restricted to that figure, however. Some contestants received considerably more, with individual payments reaching as much as $100,000.The difference between the amounts reflected the personal nature of the arrangement. There was no published scoring system, fixed eligibility requirement or predetermined share of the show's prize fund. Sia decided who she wanted to support and how much she wanted to give.The Sia Prize ended after eight years and 14 seasonsOn May 24, Jeff Probst announced through his Instagram Story that the tradition was coming to an end. His message confirmed that Sia's involvement had extended across eight years and 14 seasons, with 19 contestants receiving money and the total amount distributed exceeding $1 million.Probst acknowledged the singer's generosity and described the arrangement as an unusual relationship between a television programme and a pop star. He also recognised that the awards had brought happiness to contestants who had been selected through Sia's personal connection with their performances.The announcement marked the end of a practice that had begun with a single $50,000 gift to Tai Trang. It had subsequently developed into a recurring feature that gave contestants another opportunity for recognition, independent of the competition's final result.You use AI every day. articles.summary: A centuries-old marble bust of Sir John Gordon, once used as a doorstop in a shed, is now valued at £3.1 million. Discover its fascinating journey and the implications of a temporary export bar placed on this valuable Scottish artifact.
articles.body: In the Scottish Highlands, a marble bust of an 18th-century landowner spent years propping open a shed door. Few people paid attention to it until someone recognised its value. The small town of Invergordon had been holding a sculpture that the UK government now values at £3.1 million, according to the GOV.UK press release.Invergordon Town Council bought the bust for £5 in 1930Invergordon Town Council bought the bust at the Kindeace House sale in January 1930 for £5 and placed it in the town hall the following month, according to the provenance notes in the GOV.UK press release. The Highland Council, which holds the bust today for the Invergordon Common Good Fund, explains the thinking in its consultation announcement: Sir John Gordon was believed to be the founder of Invergordon and the intention was to show the bust in public. As mentioned in the government statement, Gordon became the Member of Parliament of Cromarty after his father and was the Secretary for Scottish Affairs to Frederick, Prince of Wales, in the 1740s.Edmé Bouchardon sculpted Sir John Gordon in RomeSmithsonian Magazine reports that Gordon met the French artist Edmé Bouchardon in Rome while travelling Europe as a young man and that Bouchardon made the marble there in 1728. The description provided by GOV.UK is that its height is 81 cm and its width is 51 cm. Moreover, this bust is described as the only one in which Bouchardon created a classicizing portrait of a Scottish nobleman. The bust then dropped out of sight. By 1998, it was serving as a doorstop in a shed, the Smithsonian report says. It was later shown at the Louvre in Paris in 2016 and the Getty in Los Angeles in 2017, as part of a Bouchardon exhibition. The Highland Council has owned it since 1999 for the Invergordon Common Good Fund, according to the provenance in the GOV.UK release.The Highland Council’s earlier consultation announcement valued this particular bust at more than £2.5 million. By January 2026, the UK Government had put the official valuation at £3.1 million, plus £620,000 in VAT that an eligible institution could reclaim. Its value made public display too expensive, so the bust stayed in a secure store.The proposed sale received council and court approval in 2024According to ARTnews, a private buyer offered more than £2.5 million for the sculpture through Sotheby’s and promised to pay for a museum-quality replica to be displayed in Invergordon. The Council statement adds that the Common Good Fund has little other property that brings in revenue, so the sale would give it capital income. People had until 15 March 2024 to respond to the consultation. By November 2024, the council and the Sheriff's Court had both backed the sale, the Scotsman reports. Neither approval settled where the bust would end up because the sale still needed an export licence.The UK placed a temporary export bar on the £3.1 million bustA Highland Council Committee paper states the application for a UK export licence was made on 12 March 2025. Objections followed and the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art looked at the Case in July 2025. It concluded that the bust met all three Waverly criteria of national importance, Rehs Galleries reports.The government announced a temporary export bar on the bust on 9 January, 2026, according to the GOV.UK press release. The recommended purchase price was £3,135,090, which includes the cost of making a replica of the bust for Invergordon. A UK institution that matches that price would keep the bust in Britain. The export licence decision was put on hold until 8 April 2026. When that first deferral period ended, the owner had 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price. The export bar put the sale on hold and gave a UK museum or gallery the chance to make an offer matching the recommended price.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Adam Hamilton's blue breakthrough flips 94 years of Red in Kansas Senate seat
articles.summary: In a state where Republican dominance had stood firm for nearly a century, a Methodist pastor has rewritten the political script.
articles.body: In a state where Republican dominance had stood firm for nearly a century, a Methodist pastor has rewritten the political script. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and founding pastor of a 25,000-member megachurch, defeated Republican Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas, ending the party’s 94-year losing streak in Senate elections and flipping a seat long considered safely Republican.Hamilton’s victory marks a historic breakthrough for Kansas Democrats, who had not won a Senate race in the state since 1932. The upset also reflects growing voter dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump, particularly over the rising cost of living, his handling of the economy and the war with Iran.The campaign became an unlikely political battleground in a traditionally Republican state.As per a report by The Associated Press, nearly $110 million was spent on the contest, setting a record for campaign spending in Kansas. Despite an aggressive Republican effort to rescue Marshall's re-election bid, including two rallies by Trump in October and multiple visits by Vice President JD Vance, Hamilton prevailed.The Democrat built his campaign around moderate Republicans and independent voters. He presented himself as an independent-minded candidate who could challenge the intense partisanship in Washington. He also promised to offer a centrist voice in the Senate.The report also maps how Hamilton's fundraising proved another major advantage.His campaign significantly outpaced Marshall's, particularly in contributions from Kansas residents. Democratic groups invested tens of millions of dollars in the race. According to ad-tracking firm AdImpact, Republicans spent $45 million on television and digital advertisements, while Democrats spent $65 million. Democratic groups alone spent more than $27 million on such advertisements in the second half of October.Republicans tried to counter Hamilton's growing appeal by portraying him as too liberal for Kansas. Vance called him “Chuck Schumer’s stooge” during a visit to Topeka. Hamilton, however, repeatedly said he would not support retaining the New York senator as Democratic leader.He also sought to distance himself from the party's more liberal positions. During an event in Topeka, Hamilton criticised US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), but stopped short of calling for its abolition.“They were formed to make sure that people didn’t fly aeroplanes into buildings again,” he said, referencing the September 11 terror attacks. “If they stick to what they were created for, I’m grateful for them.”A pastor enters political history booksHamilton is the founding pastor of the Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas City area. With around 25,000 members, it is the largest United Methodist congregation in the US. He brought to the campaign a public profile as a religious leader, an established fundraising network and a record as the author of several dozen books.His victory breaks a political drought that had become part of Kansas' electoral history. The last Democrat to win a Senate race in the state was Wichita attorney George McGill in 1932. Since then, Republicans have maintained an exceptionally strong hold over Senate elections.The closest contest in decades came in 1974, when Republican icon Bob Dole won a second term by less than two percentage points. The election followed the Watergate scandal that forced then-President Richard Nixon to resign.Yet Kansas has never been entirely immune to Democratic victories. While often regarded as a deeply Republican state, it has a sizeable bloc of moderate voters who have regularly helped Democrats win gubernatorial elections. Suburbs near Kansas City, Missouri, have also become increasingly favourable to Democrats. This has given the party a stronger route to statewide victories.Marshall's loyalty to Trump fails to save his seatMarshall, a retired obstetrician, was elected to the House of Representatives in 2017 before winning his Senate seat in 2020. He remained a staunch Trump ally throughout the campaign, defending the president's handling of the economy, tariffs and the war with Iran.Trump held rallies for Marshall on October 19 and October 31. Vance also campaigned for him in September and returned to Kansas on October 26.Republicans warned voters that electing Hamilton would put liberal Democrats in control of the Senate. But the message failed to overcome concerns about the economy and the growing cost of living.Marshall also faced criticism over allegations that he had abandoned Kansas to live in Florida. He said he owned a holiday home there to spend time with his family. He sold the property last month.Another line of attack concerned his medical practice. The New York Times reported that Marshall and his practice had sued more than 700 patients over unpaid bills during his medical career. In 81 cases, patients were arrested after missing court dates. Two experts described the tactics as extreme. Marshall rejected the criticism during a televised debate, calling the attacks a “gross mischaracterisation” of his professional record.Hamilton's church also came under scrutiny over two alleged sexual abuse incidents involving teenage boys at its annual camps in 2005 and 2006. The church investigated the first incident but did not report it to law enforcement because the victims could not positively identify the alleged perpetrator. The man returned for the following year's camp.The second incident was reported to law enforcement. The church also handed over its records on the first case, but the local prosecutor did not pursue criminal charges.The church subsequently changed its child protection policies and made reporting all incidents to law enforcement mandatory. Hamilton acknowledged that it was a mistake not to report the first incident in 2005 and that he had failed to personally check whether the man had returned the following year.Despite these controversies and the Republican campaign against him, Hamilton's centrist pitch and the wider discontent with Trump helped him cross a political divide that had kept Kansas Democrats out of the Senate for 94 years.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1944, a US Navy serviceman stationed in the Pacific mailed his wife a coconut with their names carved inside a heart; he paid 37 cents in postage, and she kept it for more than 50 years
articles.summary: Strawberries are popularised as one of the most romantic fruits in the world.
articles.body: Strawberries are popularised as one of the most romantic fruits in the world. Not only do they look like little red hearts, their history dates back to Ancient Rome where it was considered the symbol of Venus, the goddess of love, because of its bright red colour and intoxicating taste.But, what if I tell you, one of the most romantic stories is that of coconuts?It was back in 1944. Marie Boudet had received mail. Surprisingly, she found a coconut. It was sent by her husband, Raymond, who was currently a US Navy serviceman stationed in Hawaii during the Second World war. A closer inspection led her to discover something heartwarming.Carved into the back of the giant seed pod was a heart pierced by an arrow, with the names Ray and Marie nestled inside it. The message was accompanied by another inscription, marking the Seabees' presence in the Hawaiian Islands between 1943 and 1944. A paper decal of a hula girl playing the ukulele added a rather tropical touch to the love letter.The front of the coconut was addressed to Mrs R. Boudet in Springfield, Massachusetts. Raymond had even attached the postage tag himself, wiring it to the fruit before sending it off. The postage cost 37 cents and was canceled by the U.S. Navy, the Navy Censor, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The stamps are from the 1938 Presidential Series: a seven cent Jackson and two fifteen cent Buchanan stamps.Its return address indicated that the coconut had travelled by naval ship, through the Fleet Post Office in San Francisco, California, before making its way to his wife.A little love, courtesy of the SeabeesRaymond was a member of the 99th Naval Construction Battalion, Company A, popularly known as the Seabees. These construction battalions were responsible for building and repairing naval aviation bases, shore facilities and other military infrastructure during the war. Their insignia, depicting a bee holding construction tools and surrounded by anchors, was also affixed to Marie's coconut.Raymond spent around a year and a half stationed in Hawaii before being deployed to the Philippines, on the island of Samar. His battalion was tasked with building a hospital camp in preparation for treating wounded American soldiers who might return from a potential Japanese invasion.With much of his time spent away from home, the coconut was a rather unconventional way of sending a little reminder of himself across the Pacific. It was neither conventional, nor was it a particularly easy object to slip into an envelope. But then again, love letters need not always follow postal etiquette.When coconuts became postcardsSending unusual objects through the postal service is hardly a modern phenomenon. Since the introduction of parcel post in 1913, people have found rather creative ways to use the service, mailing everything from food and animals to objects that would otherwise seem entirely unsuitable for a postman's bag.In fact, the postal service was once even used to send children. In one well-known incident in 1913, an Ohio couple sent their eight-month-old son to his grandmother through the mail because it was cheaper than purchasing a train ticket. The baby weighed just under the parcel limit, and his journey cost his parents only 15 cents. Regulations prohibiting the mailing of people were introduced soon after, putting an end to what was perhaps the most literal interpretation of special delivery.Coconuts, however, have enjoyed a much longer postal career. Sending an unwrapped coconut through the mail remains legal, making it something of a novelty in the Hawaiian Islands. Tourists can still send coconut postcards to friends and family on the mainland, often with a little message and a wish-you-were-here sentiment carved or written onto the fruit.Unlike the usual postcard that gets tucked away in a drawer, these tropical souvenirs arrive with their own natural packaging. They are also considerably harder to mistake for junk mail.A marriage that lasted longer than the coconutRaymond's unusual love letter eventually found a home in the collection of the Smithsonian's National Postal Museum. When Marie donated the coconut, she included a note about the keepsake and the marriage it represented.The couple had married in 1942, when they were both just 19 years old. Raymond returned safely from the war, and their marriage lasted for another 53 years. Marie reflected on how the coconut had survived for so long, much like their relationship, which had weathered the distance and uncertainty of wartime.There is something rather lovely about ordinary things becoming the ones you cherish the most. Raymond's coconut travelled thousands of miles, carrying a small declaration of love from a serviceman stationed overseas to his young wife back home. More than half a century later, it was still around to tell their story.Strawberries may have the reputation, but perhaps coconuts deserve a little recognition in the romance department, too.You use AI every day. articles.title: Friend, 2 aides strangle Delhi property dealer over suspected affair, stuff body in bag
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A 30-year-old property dealer was strangled, allegedly by three men, over suspicions of an illicit relationship in southwest Delhi's Dabri area
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A 30-year-old property dealer was strangled, allegedly by three men, over suspicions of an illicit relationship in southwest Delhi's Dabri area last week. According to police, the suspects stuffed his body inside a bag, tied his hands with ropes, locked the flat and fled. Two of them have been arrested.The victim, Vinod, was a resident of Chhawla. According to preliminary investigation, he was invited for dinner to Bengali Colony, Mahavir Enclave, by his friend Yogesh alias Tinku on Oct 31 evening. Police said after dinner, Yogesh, along with his brother-in-law Munchun and their friend Chandan, allegedly strangled Vinod, put his body in a bag and left.Dabri police received information about the incident around 12.30pm Monday, following which the SHO, along with other cops, reached the spot and discovered Vinod's body.Police subsequently apprehended Yogesh alias Tinku (28) and Munchun (25). Munchun has been previously involved in theft and burglary cases, according to police. While Yogesh is educated up to Class XII, Munchun has studied up to Class VII. Chandan is absconding.According to investigators, Yogesh suspected Vinod of having an illicit relationship with his wife Shobha, who works in event management. During interrogation, he claimed Vinod had been speaking about his wife in derogatory terms. Yogesh also told cops that Vinod had loaned him some money to buy an air-conditioner and was now demanding it back. Police are verifying these claims.While police suspect an argument may have escalated into a physical scuffle on the day of the murder, they are also examining the evidence to ascertain if the crime was a premeditated one. "We are probing if the murder was being planned for weeks," a police source said.Meanwhile, the crime team and forensic science laboratory experts have inspected the crime scene and collected evidence, and the body has been sent for a post-mortem. A case under BNS Section 103(1) (murder) has been registered at Dabri police station. articles.title: In 1992, a trucker paid $5 for a drip painting at a San Bernardino thrift shop; a fingerprint said Pollock, experts said no, and she died in 2019 refusing $50 million
articles.summary: In 1992, Teri Horton bought an oil painting for $5 at a thrift shop, igniting a decades-long debate over its connection to Jackson Pollock. Despite forensic evidence, experts dispute its authenticity. Horton declined offers up to $50 million before her death in 2019, leaving the painting's origins shrouded in mystery.
articles.body: An oil painting purchased at a thrift store in California for $5 dollars, sparked a legal battle over its provenance as a work by the most famous American abstract painter. Teri Horton, a truck driver from California, purchased the painting to give it as a present to a friend. At the time, she had no idea that the artwork might be an original painting by Jackson Pollock, whose works have sold for millions of dollars. The story started in 1992; however, arguments about the painting’s origins have gone on far beyond that year. Although forensic art expert Paul Biro claimed that a fingerprint on the painting matched one found on a paint can in Pollock’s former studio, the evidence did not establish that Pollock had created the artwork.A $5 thrift shop purchase led to an unexpected discovery According to the Los Angeles Times, Horton bought the 66-by-48-inch painting for $5 at Dot’s Thrift Shop in San Bernardino, California, in 1992. Her plan was to give the canvas to her friend. However, it was too big to pass through the entrance of her friend's trailer. Later on, she decided to sell the canvas at a yard sale. Upon observing the canvas, an art teacher proposed that the artwork could be one of Pollock’s works. Initially, Horton was unaware of Pollock as an artist. Nevertheless, the suggestion urged her to find out more about it. He became popular by using drips, pours and splashes of paint on huge canvases. It seemed reasonable due to Pollock's style. However, the only thing visual similarities could not prove was the painter.A fingerprint examination pointed towards Pollock’s studio Eventually, Horton contacted forensic art expert Paul Biro from Canada. During his examination, Biro reported finding a partial fingerprint in paint on the back of the canvas. According to CNN’s 2007 report, Biro compared the fingerprint found on the back of Horton’s canvas with one he identified on a paint can in Pollock’s former studio in East Hampton, New York. Biro claimed that the partial fingerprints on the canvas matched a print on a paint can from Pollock’s former East Hampton studio. He argued that the match connected the painting to the artist’s studio, although he did not independently establish Pollock as its creator. André Turcotte, a retired fingerprint examiner with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, supported Biro’s fingerprint comparison.However, apart from studying the prints, Biro analysed the paintings, material composition and condition as well. According to his conclusion, the painting had enough similarities to be made by Pollock, but this conclusion didn’t confirm the artist's authenticity without doubt. After consulting a team of Pollock specialists, IFAR concluded that the painting was not by Jackson Pollock. According to CBS News, IFAR’s expert acknowledged that the painting had some strong similarities to authentic Pollock works, but concluded that it was not by his hand.Art specialists rejected the Pollock attributionIFAR tested the painting and sought the views of experts acquainted with Pollock’s style of painting. After consulting a team of Pollock’s specialists, there were issues related to provenance that added more complications to the case.The painting had no signature and had no ownership history linking it to Pollock. By the time Horton started investigating the painting's origin, Dot’s Thrift Shop had been torn down and its owner had died. It was hard for anyone to trace the origins of the painting or know how it came into the hands of the owners of the thrift shop.Horton declined millions, but never sold the paintingNevertheless, Horton was sure that the canvas was authentic. There is a difference in the reports about the potential buyers’ offers; CBS reported that there was at least one art collector willing to pay $2 million, while the Los Angeles Times mentioned the art dealers as the source of the offer. Horton also reportedly rejected a $9 million offer from a Saudi collector, according to The New Yorker. In a 2007 interview with CBS News, Horton said she believed the painting was worth at least $50 million, although no independent valuation or confirmed offer of that amount was established. This amount referred to the price, which she expected from the sale of the canvas. The story became well known through the documentary film Who the $&% Is Jackson Pollock? That described her attempts to prove the authenticity of the work. Horton passed away on July 8, 2019, being 86 years old. At the time of her death, the artist of the canvas was not established. It remained disputable and unauthenticated and there was no conclusion about the artist who created it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
